newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Andreotti was target of plot - witness.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Andreotti was target of plot - witness.

text.p: Former prime minister Giulio Andreotti, on trial for alleged links with the Mafia, was the target of a "cloak and dagger" plot by one of Italy's top crimefighters, a witness testified on Wednesday.

Angelo Incandela, a retired senior prison officer, told the court in the Sicilian capital Palermo that the late Carlo Alberto Dalla Chiesa, a Carabinieri paramilitary police general, had tried to plant evidence and was "obsessed" with Andreotti.
Incandela quoted Dalla Chiesa as saying several times: "To serve the country we sometimes need to commit illegal acts."
Dalla Chiesa was hailed as a hero after he was shot dead with his wife in 1982 in one of the Mafia's worst outrages shortly after he was sent to Palermo to lead the fight against organised crime.

He had previously broken the back of Red Brigades urban guerrilla violence, which reached its peak with the kidnapping and murder of Christian Democrat leader Aldo Moro in 1978 during one of Andreotti's seven terms as prime minister.
Incandela said he had bugged cells of Red Brigades members on Dalla Chiesa's behalf, but did not listen to the tapes.

"In particular, Dalla Chiesa always asked me whether any of the inmates had talked about Andreotti, whether the senator had taken an interest in any of them and whether any politician had visited inmates in jails," Incandela said.
"One day he confided in me that he did not trust Andreotti."
Incandela said that Dalla Chiesa had asked him in 1981 to plant a typewritten document in a prison water closet.

"These concern our friend. Put them behind a cistern in the prisoners' common room, order a search and when you've found it write a report and send it to me," Incandela quoted Dalla Chiesa as telling him.
It was not clear when the incident occurred or what the papers said. Incandela told the court he had refused to carry out the operation because it was unfeasible.
Andreotti, a life senator who turned 78 on Tuesday, denies charges that he was the Mafia's main protector in the Rome corridors of power in exchange for support in Sicily.
He told reporters at the court that Incandela's testimony was "mind-boggling".
"The fact that Dalla Chiesa seems to have wanted to plant documents so they would be found...sounds like a mystery novel," the former Christian Democrat said.

Moro's killing remains one of the murkiest chapters in Italy's post-war history. The government refused to negotiate to obtain his release and speculation has continued to swirl that the kidnappers may have had high-level backers.
